problem: Zero-shot VLN-CE methods either depend on a pre-trained waypoint predictor that generalizes poorly to unseen scenes and limits backtracking, or use value-mapping with VLMs that confines large models to offline instruction parsing and underuses their reasoning during navigation.
motivation: A purely zero-shot VLN-CE framework should drop the waypoint predictor and use MLLM reasoning online at every step. Navigation decisions differ in granularity (strategic planning, perceptual grounding, motor control), so the paper argues each should go to a different model scale.
key_idea: Decompose navigation into a coarse-to-fine action hierarchy (Language Action by a large MLLM, Vision Action by a smaller MLLM, Robot Action by a rule-based controller), translating from language to pixel to pose.
insight: Pairing a strong planner with a smaller grounding model works best: GPT-4o for both stages drops SPL from 28.3 to 16.8, and Qwen-72B as planner drops SPL by 7.0 points. Removing LA (SPL 4.4), VA (13.9) or both (0.0) shows each level of the hierarchy is necessary. Raw visual history plus actions, flexible backtracking, and bbox bottom-center pixel selection each add several SPL points.
method: Language Action: a large MLLM (GPT-4o or Gemini-2.5-Pro) takes the instruction, four-view observation (front/left/right/back) and the visual+action history. It outputs a progress estimation and a discrete action: navigate to <direction>, backtrack to <waypoint>, or stop.

Vision Action: a smaller MLLM (Qwen2.5-VL-32B) receives the instruction, the progress estimation and the single image in the chosen direction. It outputs a 2D bounding box and a target description, prompted to pick a target that is not too close.
Robot Action: the bottom-center pixel of the bbox is unprojected with depth and intrinsics, then transformed to a world 2D map position using the agent pose.

Path planning and control: Fast Marching Method on a depth-built global map gives a short-term path, and a low-level controller executes it with local obstacle avoidance. Swapping the controller adapts to different robots.
Navigation history and backtracking: history stores past observations and actions, and any previously visited waypoint can be a backtrack target.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o or Gemini-2.5-Pro (frozen, planner) + Qwen2.5-VL-32B (frozen, grounding) + rule-based FMM controller
setting.action_space: language directions/backtrack/stop -> pixel target -> projected world waypoint executed by FMM low-level control in continuous space
setting.privileged: none (agent pose/odometry assumed available for mapping)

results: On the 100-episode VLN-CE val-unseen subset, LaViRA (Gemini-2.5-Pro) reaches SR 38.3 / SPL 28.3, beating the best prior zero-shot InstructNav (SR 31, SPL 24.0) by 7.3 SR and 4.3 SPL. Its SR also exceeds some supervised methods (RecBERT 48 and ETPNav 52 are higher, so this holds only for CMA 37). The GPT-4o variant reaches SR 36.0 / SPL 28.3, and the cost is about $0.084 per episode.
limitations: Relies on proprietary MLLM APIs (latency, cost, stability); performance is bounded by off-the-shelf models, with failures on ambiguous instructions and large-area grounding.
Evaluated only on a 100-episode subset with noisy results (std of several points); real-world evidence is qualitative only.
Depth errors (e.g., transparent objects) and real-world sensor noise, dynamic obstacles and drift affect the 3D projection.
